newsitem.title: USA: USDA data expected to show US hog numbers climbing.
newsitem.headline: USDA data expected to show US hog numbers climbing.

text.p: CHICAGO, June 25, Reuters - The number of hogs on U.S. farms as of June 1 have likely exceeded year-earlier levels as the industry responds to lower feed costs and expected larger pork exports, livestock analysts said.
The expansion is expected to be confirmed by Friday's U.S. Agriculture Department Hogs and Pigs Report. Data will be released at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT.
High cash hog prices since the summer of 1995, even with high corn prices last year, encouraged expansion, said Dan Vaught, livestock analyst with AG Edwards.

"I just don't think you can slaughter as few numbers of sows as we keep seeing and hear so much antidotal evidence of people holding back gilts without there being some validity to expansion ideas," Vaught said.

Analysts' estimates for all hogs and pigs on U.S. farms as of June 1 averaged 102.9 percent of a year ago and ranged from 101.7 to 105 percent. Estimates on hogs kept for breeding averaged 104.3 percent in a range of 103 to 106 percent and hogs kept for market averaged 102.6 percent of a year ago in a range of 101 to 105 pct.
Much of the expansion was expected from medium-sized producers as environmental problems, odors and legislative action continued to hamper big producers, they said.

"The lion's share of the expansion we are getting in the hog industry right now is not coming from the mega- or giant-sized producers," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst with Alaron Trading Corp.
Levitt and other analysts noted that big operations in some states were being subjected to numerous constraints which made expansion difficult even with feed costs down.

"The ones who are expanding the greatest are the middle-sized producers that have the hog facilities to expand if they wanted to and opted to sell corn last year at record high prices rather than put them through hogs. Those people are now back in the business," he said.

Corn prices have come down more than two dollars per bushel from a year ago and the hog corn ratio has gone to 22 to 1 currently from 12 to 1 a year ago. The ratio indicates how much corn is available to feed a hog.
Corn producers will run the corn through hogs this year, Levitt added.
March-May pig crop estimates averaged 103.8 percent of a year ago in a range of 101 to 106.6. The spring pig crop constitutes the bulk of final quarter slaughter this year.

Further expansion was also expected as analysts' estimates on June-August farrowing intentions averaged 104.6 percent in a range of 103 to 106.4 and September-November intentions averaged 105.9 in a range of 104 to 108 percent.
Much of the report may already be in the futures market and the data will have to be one way or the other in terms of numbers compared to the average to move futures, sources said.

"There seems to be a general attitude that expansion is starting to pick up the pace and a neutral report could end up actually, in terms of prices, being a little bit friendly (to futures) because of people's expectations," said Dale Durchholz, AgriVisor Services Inc market analyst.
But he noted that expansion may not be as great as some are anticipating.

"The increasing rate of expansion has been real small. I look around at some of these regulatory environmental problems and this may be possibly causing expansion to be occurring at a less-than-expected pace," Durchholz said.
